k013: Is everything fine? Know in one second.
k014: Dumb-simple, self-hosted monitoring from the homelab to the small business. One container, one IP address to type in, useful graphs and alerts in under a minute.
k016: Then open http://localhost:8080 and create the first account. Image for amd64 (arm64 later): ghcr.io/laupernoe/dumbmonit.
k020: The bulletin, on the wall screen of a test instance with failures switched on — the weather window is a living Paris rooftop with the pigeons. On a quiet day it reads “Clear skies.”
k021: This is an alpha (0.1.0-alpha.7 is the current release). DumbMonit runs every day on its author's own network, but the HTTP API is not frozen, the database schema still moves and there is no upgrade guarantee across schema changes yet. Several integrations have only met test instances, not years-old production hardware; they are marked below. Try it, and tell us what breaks.
k056: Useful rules are on right after install. The work goes into sending fewer, better messages.
k058: Declare a switch as the parent of what sits behind it. When it goes down you get one notification, not thirty; the others read “Suppressed by parent”.
k060: A NAS whose array degrades sends one message per cycle, not one per disk. Reminders, escalation, acknowledgement, snooze, per-device ignore and clearing resolved history are all built in.
k062: Anomaly detection with no threshold to tune: 168 buckets, one per hour of the week. It stays silent for its first 14 days and only shows what it would have fired.
k064: “This filesystem will be full within four days” is listed as a forecast, apart from what is broken right now.
k066: One-off or weekly windows, hysteresis, flap hold, quiet hours, batching and an hourly cap, so a bad night does not become two hundred pushes.
k068: Alerts, grouped by host. Severities read like a weather service: info, advisory, warning.
k070: Each one has a Test button and a setup page in the documentation.
k093: An agent for what does not speak SNMP
k094: A small binary that pushes CPU, memory, disks, network, services and uptime to the server, plus temperatures, fans, SMART and ZFS pools where the machine exposes them. It calls the server, never the other way round: no port to open on the machine.
k095: A PowerShell script is served at /install.ps1 for Windows. The agent is also an image, ghcr.io/laupernoe/dumbmonit-agent.
k098: x86_64 and aarch64, systemd or OpenRC. Docker containers and OS health (updates, pending reboot, failed units).
k100: x86_64, installed as a Windows service. SMART through smartctl.
k103: launchd, Apple silicon and Intel; binaries attached to each release. Not yet run on real hardware.
k105: rc.d, x86_64, ZFS pools. Not yet run on real hardware.
k107: In relay mode an agent runs the server's probes (SNMP, Proxmox, HTTP…) from its own network — a second site, a client's network or a VPS behind NAT — with nothing inbound: no VPN, no port to open. Monitor a remote site
k108: Status pages for the people you serve
k109: Public pages at /s/<name>: groups of services with 90 days of daily history, 30- and 90-day uptime, incident and maintenance announcements, email subscribers with double opt-in, RSS, badges for a README, a compact embed for an intranet, an optional 90-day calendar and response-time graphs, and an optional scene behind the banner: about fifty to pick from, from city skylines (Venice, Paris, Tokyo, New York…) and wonders of the world to Swiss landmarks (the Matterhorn, the Jet d’Eau, Lucerne, Bern, Chillon). The sky follows the state of your services, and each scene reacts in its own way when something goes down or comes back. The Swiss ones carry an SBB-style station clock, a split-flap alert board, fireworks on 1 August, the Escalade cauldron and winter snow.
k110: Only the labels you choose leave the server. Device names, addresses and types never appear on the page, in a badge or in an email.
k113: The bulletin alone, full screen, for a room monitor: a living scene (Paris rooftop with the Eiffel Tower and the DumbMonit pigeons by default, or one of many others) whose weather follows your alerts, an OLED theme for a screen left on for days, and wall music — Spotify Connect turns the screen into a speaker.
k115: Every supported device gets a 0–100 score and an A–F grade from the vendor’s own best-practice checks, PingCastle-style: category, severity, evidence, remediation, and a worst-first Security page.
k117: Admin, operator (handles alerts, changes no configuration) and viewer roles, optional TOTP second factor, an audit log, and single sign-on over OpenID Connect (Authentik, Authelia, Keycloak, Pocket ID…), account creation off by default.
k118: Plays well with what you run
k119: /metrics, /federate and a Prometheus-compatible endpoint let an existing Grafana read DumbMonit's data.
k121: Every route behind /api/openapi.json (OpenAPI 3.1): scoped tokens (dmt_…, read or write) that can expire, be restricted to a network, and are rate-limited. API reference
k123: 27 tools for ChatGPT, VS Code or Cursor: read status, devices, alerts, metrics and agents; a write token can also silence, acknowledge, add a device or restart a container. Secrets never come back. Connect an assistant
k125: Read the state, acknowledge an alert, start a maintenance window. Installable on the home screen, deliberately without an offline mode: it never shows yesterday's state.
k126: The same bulletin at phone width.
k153: Apache 2.0, dependencies included: CI fails on any dependency that is not under an OSI-approved licence. No feature is held back for a paid edition, because there is none.
k154: This site has no analytics, no cookies and no third-party requests.
k162: A device that reads wrong, an alert that woke you for nothing, a page that confused you: each report makes the next alpha better. Device support requests are welcome too.
k165: DumbMonit, Apache 2.0. The mascot is a pigeon.
k170: the UI fills in the token for you
k174: The DumbMonit pigeon, slate blue with googly eyes and an orange beak
k175: Wall mode: the sentence '9 warnings, 7 advisories, 2 info.', readouts for reporting devices, alerts and forecasts, a stormy weather window with the pigeon, and the alerts that need you
k179: Alerts page: firing alerts grouped under their host, each with a Warning or Advisory plate, Ack, Silence 1 h and Open device
k181: The bulletin on a phone: the sentence, readouts, the weather window with the pigeon, and the first alert that needs you

k185: DumbMonit: Is everything fine? Know in one second. Self-hosted monitoring in one container, next to the pigeon mascot.
t_home: DumbMonit: dumb-simple monitoring from the homelab to the small business
d_features: Dependency-aware alerts, @@NCHANNELS@@ notification channels, public status pages, a wall screen, agents for Linux, Windows, macOS and FreeBSD, email reports and an MCP server. Open source.
d_devices: @@NDEV@@ device types in @@NFAM@@ families: servers, switches, firewalls, hypervisors, NAS, websites, databases and self-hosted apps. What is watched, the alert rules that ship and what to prepare.

d_community: Documentation on Read the Docs, source code on GitHub, how to contribute, report a security issue or translate. Open source under Apache 2.0.
hl1_p: A single container with one volume and no extra capability. Open the page, create an account, add a device: graphs and alerts follow.
hl2_p: Useful rules are on from the start. Dependencies, grouping and learned baselines turn thirty messages into one.
hl3_p: Switches, firewalls, hypervisors, NAS, websites, databases and self-hosted apps, each read the way its vendor intends.
hl4_t: Status pages and a wall screen
hl4_p: Share a public status page with your users, or put the weather-report view on a screen in the room.
home_dev_p: Pick a family to see what is watched, the alert rules that come with it and what to prepare on the device.
home_cta_p: Three commands, or look at the live demo first.
f_lede: Alerting, status pages, agents and the rest, in one container. What each kind of device reports is on the Devices pages.
f_rep_p: A short weekly email (or daily, or monthly) with availability by group, the incidents of the period and the least stable devices, sent without anyone opening DumbMonit.
f_topo_p: One picture of the whole infrastructure, drawn from what DumbMonit already knows: dependencies, relays, hypervisor guests and LLDP neighbours. Nothing to type in by hand.

f_lang_p: English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese (Portugal and Brazil), Russian and Simplified Chinese: the interface, this site and the documentation. Some translations are still partial.

in_s2_p: Docker pulls the image and starts DumbMonit together with its time-series database.

co_tr_p: Translations are made by pull request, for the interface, the documentation and this site.

fam_servers_blurb: Linux, Windows, macOS and FreeBSD machines through the agent, server hardware through its management controller, UPS units and Active Directory.
fam_network_blurb: Switches, routers, access points and VPNs: any SNMP device, MikroTik, UniFi, Tailscale and OpenVPN.
fam_firewalls_blurb: OPNsense, pfSense, FortiGate and Sophos: gateways, tunnels, interfaces, high availability and licences.
fam_hypervisors_blurb: Proxmox, vSphere, XCP-ng, Nutanix and Kubernetes: hosts, guests, storage and cluster health.
fam_storage_blurb: Synology, TrueNAS, Unraid, Proxmox Backup Server and Veeam: disks, pools, and the age of the last good backup.
fam_checks_blurb: Web pages and APIs, ports, DNS, ping, TLS certificates, time servers, domain expiry, heartbeats and website changes.
fam_proxies_blurb: Traefik, Caddy, Nginx, Apache and Nginx Proxy Manager: backends, certificates and error rates.
fam_apps_blurb: Nextcloud, Immich, Paperless-ngx, Jellyfin, Plex, Home Assistant, GitLab and Forgejo.
fam_mail_blurb: Pi-hole, AdGuard Home, CrowdSec, and the mail servers and gateways: SMTP, MDaemon, SecurityGateway and Proxmox Mail Gateway.
fam_data_blurb: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, RabbitMQ, MQTT, and the VictoriaMetrics, Loki and Graylog servers.
